book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

chapters.file: ch162 - It’s Just that Demon Life Has Got Me in Its Sway.md
chapters.relation: Reads "Sympathy for the Devil" through Saint Augustine's Confessions rather than only through Bulgakov's Master and Margarita, which supposedly inspired the lyrics. Augustine's stolen pears and his confession that he loved evil "solely because it was evil" show him needing "the companionship of others sinning," which the chapter pairs with the song's "Who killed the Kennedys?... It was you and me" and with Lee Harvey Oswald's refusal to have acted alone. But the paths split: Jagger's Devil makes evil real and ours, while for Augustine evil has no positive existence at all.

chapters.file: ch163 - It’s Only Rock’n’Roll, But I Complicate It.md
chapters.relation: Casts Augustine as the first Christian rock artist — a rebellious, sex-obsessed convert who, like Plato, ranked the body below the soul — and explains his privation doctrine: "evil has no positive nature; but the loss of good has received the name 'evil.'" Evil is "a swerving of the will which is turned toward lower things," so free will is crucial: God permits evil because virtues like courage could not exist in a world without it. The chapter closes with the constellation of opposites (soul/body, pride/humility, temporal/eternal) Augustine says we must live through to approach philosophical truth.

chapters.file: ch164 - I Shouted Out, Who Killed Meredith Hunter.md
chapters.relation: Takes the refrain "what's puzzling you is the nature of my game" to mean the song presents the Devil as a real, personal force present at the crucifixion, the Russian Revolution, World War II and the Kennedy assassinations — not the mere lack of goodness Augustine allows. It cites Richards's 2002 remark, on the heels of 9/11, that confronting evil puts him "out of a job," and reads "Sweet Neo Con" as Jagger still indicting ideology. Against Augustine's weak-willed sinner, "every cop is a criminal" locates evil in human strength and resolve — with Godard's Eve Democracy answering "Yes" to "Is the Devil God in exile?"

chapters.file: ch165 - Under Our Thumb.md
chapters.relation: Corrects the popular error that Meredith Hunter was killed while "Sympathy for the Devil" played: eyewitnesses and the Gimme Shelter footage show the murder happened during "Under My Thumb" at the Altamont free concert of December 6, 1969. It surveys the assigning of blame — Rolling Stone captioning Jagger's picture "Is Mick responsible for the killing?", Norma Coates blaming the era's burden on the counterculture — and concludes Jagger sides against Augustine's privation view: Hunter did not die "at the hands of a bunch of privations," since the evil the band saw was an in-your-face reality.

chapters.file: ch166 - A Wild Murder Couldn’t Drag Me Away.md
chapters.relation: Draws Augustine and Jagger together as brothers who fell far before finding restraint: Augustine's many conflicting wills must collapse into one good will by actually choosing, and his Manichean past taught him some truths must be performed or willed, like his "grant me chastity — just not yet." The chapter reads Gimme Shelter as likewise double — harrowing documentary or joyous concert footage, forced to choose — and argues the post-Altamont Stones had to make "Sympathy for the Devil" a performative force for understanding evil rather than a scapegoat, then stayed in the flesh, confronting good and evil through the blues.

chapters.file: ch167 - Chapter 21 - Lucifer Rising and Falling.md
chapters.relation: Opens Dan Dinello's chapter with Richards's 1971 "Everybody's Lucifer" and sets up its two rival accounts of evil: the Christian Satan enshrined by Augustine — Lucifer expelled for prideful disobedience, seducing God's weak-willed children into sin — and the moral authorities of the 1960s (press, police, clergy) who cast the Stones as "Satan's Jesters" luring youth astray. The Stones answered with a nineteenth-century Romantic Lucifer, the rebellious angel fighting moral repression, blaming the mob of hypocritical authorities for the world's horrors.

chapters.file: ch168 - Diabolical Beginnings.md
chapters.relation: Traces the "devil's music" pedigree from the blues (Elmore James, Howlin' Wolf, Robert Johnson's crossroads legend) into the Stones' cultivated notoriety — urine arrests, drug busts, "Satisfaction" as an anthem against authority, "Let's Spend the Night Together" scandalizing the London Palladium. It catalogs the establishment's hysteria (Daily Mirror, Chicago Daily News) and closes with Allan Bloom's The Closing of the American Mind, which calls Jagger a nihilist "demon" and "satyr" who "legitimated drugs" and was "beyond the law, moral and political."

chapters.file: ch169 - From Satyrs to Martyrs.md
chapters.relation: Shows how Augustine forged the machinery of Christian evil — sex as sin, the invention of Original Sin, The City of God's mandate to compel heretics, and the goat-god Pan as Satan's visual model — then maps it onto the 1960s persecution of the Stones: press mockery, police drug busts, Bill Wyman hauled into court as a "shaggy monster." The persecution backfired, making the Stones martyrs and pushing Jagger toward the self-embraced "Lucifers of Rock" image of "Paint It, Black" and the Their Satanic Majesties Request cover.

chapters.file: ch170 - Invocation of My Demon Brother.md
chapters.relation: Connects the Stones' demonic turn to the counterculture's occult fashions — the Levitate the Pentagon rally, Rosemary's Baby — and to filmmaker Kenneth Anger, disciple of Aleister Crowley, whose "Do What Thou Wilt" law espoused a form of anarchism and whose Lucifer was the light-bearing god, not Christianity's dark devil. Anger cast Jagger as a latter-day Lucifer for Lucifer Rising (with Richards as Beelzebub), and the chapter quotes Jagger's 1967 claim that the teenage "telepathy" at his shows was "a protest against the system," while reading "Jumpin' Jack Flash" through the Spring Heeled Jack folklore.

chapters.file: ch171 - Flowers of Evil.md
chapters.relation: Expounds the Romantic conception of evil the Stones projected: reacting to the French, American and Industrial revolutions, William Blake's Marriage of Heaven and Hell made Satan a symbol of energy, creativity and liberation from oppressive reason — "the road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom" — while Charles Baudelaire's Flowers of Evil found in Satan a figure of political revolution and dark, seductive beauty. Like "Sympathy for the Devil," Flowers of Evil was misread as satanic: Baudelaire's real claim is that humans, not Satan, created hell on earth, and externalizing evil as a mythological creature stops us confronting and defeating it within ourselves.

chapters.file: ch172 - The Devil Is My Name.md
chapters.relation: Reports Jagger's own genealogy of the song — "an old idea of Baudelaire's," Bulgakov's Master and Margarita (given to him by Marianne Faithfull), and his Lucifer Rising conversations with Kenneth Anger — and follows its studio metamorphosis from country dirge to voodoo samba under Godard's camera. The finished recording, whose working title was "The Devil is My Name," builds into a celebration of humanity's hatred and hypocrisy from the crucifixion through the Blitzkrieg to the Kennedys (pluralized when RFK was shot on June 5, 1968, during the sessions), putting humanity on trial by the devil rather than the other way around.

chapters.file: ch173 - Lucifer’s Dream Ends.md
chapters.relation: Narrates the collapse of the Lucifer project through 1968-69: "Street Fighting Man" banned as incitement to violence after Mayor Daley's police beat protestors, Jagger reading Shelley's "Adonais" at Hyde Park after Brian Jones's death, and Anger salvaging Invocation of My Demon Brother from the stalled film. At Altamont the Hell's Angels stabbed Meredith Hunter during "Under My Thumb" while Jagger pleaded "just cool out"; Lester Bangs blamed egoism, hype and greed rather than the devil, and the Stones survived by trading rage and chaos for controlled spectacle — from Rock Satans to a knighted Elder Statesman of Rock.

chapters.file: ch174 - Chapter 22 - Frenzy.md
chapters.relation: Opens Randall Auxier's chapter with the 2011 Vancouver Stanley Cup riot and its viral kissing-couple photograph to pose the driving question: why do built-up group emotion, sex and violence fuse so explosively, and why does that fusion in public still "get yourself in trouble with the Man"? The contrast is pointed: the laid-back West Coast crowd "right across the Bay from hippie central" couldn't get through a 1969 Stones concert without violence and death — "It's just a shot away, you know?"

chapters.file: ch175 - Please Allow Me to Introduce Myself.md
chapters.relation: Confesses that Brian Jones — violent and cruel even in Keith Richards's autobiography, with no kind words from Mick and Charlie on the fortieth anniversary of his death — is for Auxier the face of the Sixties' negative energy and the figure "laughing with delight" in Don McLean's "American Pie" verse on Altamont. The section sets up the whole chapter as a meditation on "what gets sacrificed on the altar of rock'n'roll, when the Dionysian frenzy turns ugly."

chapters.file: ch176 - The Nature of My Game.md
chapters.relation: Distinguishes the individual craziness of a Brian Jones (and perhaps Meredith Hunter waving his pistol at Altamont) from the crowd frenzy that takes over when the Stones play, quoting Richards's Life memories of girls who "lost themselves" — "beyond what they wanted to be... You stood as much chance in a fucking river full of piranhas." Richards says "the music might be the trigger, but the bullet, nobody knows what that is"; Auxier argues the Stones deliberately crafted personae and performances that tap a deep human susceptibility to frenzy, and goes hunting for the bullet.

chapters.file: ch177 - Reading the Riot Act.md
chapters.relation: Reads Stones-concert riots — the Wisbech Corn Exchange brawl Richards recounts in Life — against the British Riot Act of 1714 and the purely aesthetic riot at the pagan ballet The Rite of Spring in 1913, noting conventional crowds forgive a sports brawl more readily than a Stones tragedy. In every such release of mass emotion there is a moment when "all order has disappeared and we come face to face with... whatever it is 'we' are without that imposed order," leaving nothing for memory to hang on — and the chapter insists the scary tone of violence formed around the Stones in a way it never did around Beatlemania.

chapters.file: ch178 - A Little Help from Their Friends.md
chapters.relation: Argues the frenzy needed "a little help from their friends": on the first US tour nobody knew the band and nothing happened — even in Texas — until manager Andrew Oldham planted screaming teens in a New York audience, giving crowds "a context and a clue" to abandon decorum. The Led Zeppelin comparison — same dark blues, sex and drugs, but no riots — suggests the times made the frenzy possible, yet the chapter still holds the Stones pushed collective emotion past "the line between light and dark."

chapters.file: ch179 - Gimme that Old Time Religion.md
chapters.relation: Carries the frenzy back to the Eleusinian Mysteries and the Dionysian festivals that were falling into ill repute by Plato's day: Socrates himself was an initiate, and Plato wrote on how eros makes humans "mad with passion," whitewashed his teacher in the Symposium, and claimed Socrates never got drunk. Plato also held that certain kinds of music ignite desire and lead to weakness and "effeminacy," associating manliness with rational self-restraint and advocating banning such modes — in short, "no Stones concert allowed in Plato's city."

chapters.file: ch180 - I’ve Been Around for a Long, Long Year.md
chapters.relation: Argues ritual — music, dance and sex at its core — long predates writing, citing the 10,000 B.C.E. site of Gobekli Tepe, and that fertility cults slid into human and animal sacrifice, fusing sex and death in ways "we don't like to look at." It introduces Georges Bataille's "accursed share" — the surplus energy of big-brained, bored humans — and his uncomfortably clinical account of the proximity of death and sensual desire as the frame for the Stones' debauchery, "more of an upgraded resurgence" of the cults than a degraded echo.

chapters.file: ch181 - I’m in Need of Some Restraint.md
chapters.relation: Tells how the Abraham and Isaac story introduced "redemption," a substitution rite that curbed the "pride of place" of first-borns while replacing human sacrifice — a transition the Egyptians and Greeks also made independently. Using Shirley Jackson's "The Lottery," the volunteering Druid victims and the martyr Perpetua, it argues any horror can be normalized by piety and tradition — Sarah Palin or Michele Bachmann would have defended first-born sacrifice in ancient Ur — and needles the reader with ritual chicken sacrifice versus KFC: "which of those two, in a just world, would really be more inhumane?"

chapters.file: ch182 - Stole Many a Man’s Soul and Faith.md
chapters.relation: Extends the normalization point to the present: Mel Gibson's Apocalypto versus his own gory Passion of the Christ, and the Eucharist as "eating the god," a pagan survival in Christianity that conventional believers consume on Sundays. It identifies the underlying need as "enthusiasm" — the transcendent build-up of group emotion aimed at gods, the Dallas Cowboys or the Rolling Stones — which the mainline churches killed and declined over, Pentecostal revivals and soccer matches feed, and "everybody everywhere" gets at a Stones concert.

chapters.file: ch183 - Use All Your Well-learned Politesse.md
chapters.relation: Sets Johann Jakob Bachofen's ruined-reputation matriarchy hypothesis (and Marija Gimbutas's "civilization of the goddess") against patriarchal control, finding the division alive in the male insecurity displayed whenever men prance for girls — Elvis, the Beatles and the Stones alike. Bachofen's young friend Friedrich Nietzsche named the two energies: Apollonian regimentation and order versus Dionysian overflow, "the accursed share," and the chapter reads the 1960s as one more Dionysian break-out that the "heavy-handed, patriarchal Cold War" could not bottle up.

chapters.file: ch184 - Mother’s Little Helpers.md
chapters.relation: Introduces the Cambridge scholar Jane Ellen Harrison, whose books trace Greek religion from a swampy matriarchy to the Olympian age, with Dionysus as the holy child of the Mother — flayed and divided among the faithful — the very pattern Christianity retold in the Jesus story. Auxier credits Jagger's "keen intellect" and wide sense of history, then endorses Nietzsche's complaint that Christianity is "a puny, slave morality" that renders humanity effeminate: "That's exactly what I like about Christianity," since over-weaning masculinity needs opposing.

chapters.file: ch185 - Won’t You Guess My Name.md
chapters.relation: Riffs on Harrison's Themis to cast Mick as Kouros, the golden boy served by the Kouretes — "the original name of the Rolling Stones" — until he surfaces as Dionysus among the Olympians, "sort of like the irony of Mick Jagger becoming a Knight of the Realm." It splits the males into orgy-tolerant girly-men and woman-hating "manly men" of the Sour Grapes Clubs, warns not to underestimate the girly-men, and contrasts Elvis, who went into the army and became acceptable, with Mick, who kept the Kouretes under his thumb — deliberately feminine, dangerous, and cooler than the Beatles.

chapters.file: ch186 - “They’re So Ugly It’s Appealing”.md
chapters.relation: Takes the screaming fan's verdict ("They're so ugly it's appealing") and Ian Stewart's sidelining for looking "like a man" as evidence the Stones deliberately cultivated an androgynous ugliness to violate gendered expectations — "they weren't just a bunch of guys who bent the rules, they were off-sides." The blatant misogyny of the lyrics is read as compensation for that effeminacy among the Dionysian libation bearers in a patriarchal age, keeping the manly men at arm's length — while noting only Brian Jones actually abused women.

chapters.file: ch187 - Pleased to Meet You.md
chapters.relation: Blames "the Father of All Pissing Contests" — the Cold War — for forcing English boys who love women into songs hostile to them ("Under My Thumb," "Stupid Girl," "Yesterday's Papers"), and argues two theses: the Stones don't hate women, this culture hates women; and the men who call the goddess's servants "fags" are the ones who built and maintain that misogynistic culture. The Dionysian frenzy of the 1960s took a dark turn as 1968's death toll (Vietnam, MLK, RFK) exposed the world the manly men had built: the Beatles quit, "but the Stones looked the demon square in the eye and guessed its name."

chapters.file: ch188 - From Woodstock to Altamont.md
chapters.relation: Crowns the Stones' prophetic 1969 tour, ending at Altamont, as "the genuine Dionysian frenzy" that ended the Sixties — Woodstock being merely "a glorious and well-deserved vacation from the bullshit" — and reads Brian Jones's death as his own choosing, empires falling "for about the same reasons." Auxier recalls his father taking him to Gimme Shelter in Memphis, the movie that permanently formed his refusal of the patriarchy, and advises parents to make a friend of Mick Jagger, since "Dionysus will have his day" and will take his accursed share of your kids sooner or later.

holes.name: The Romantic Satan (the rebel Lucifer)
holes.what: The nineteenth-century Romantic idea of Lucifer as a heroic rebel against tyrannical authority — a symbol of creativity, energy and liberation rather than corruption.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire arc contrasts Augustine's Satan with the Romantic Lucifer the Stones embraced, a conception developed by Blake and Baudelaire that no existing taxonomy slug covers.

holes.name: Allan Bloom
holes.what: Conservative political philosopher whose The Closing of the American Mind attacks rock music, calling Jagger a nihilist "demon" and "satyr" who legitimated drugs and thumbed his nose at moral and political law.
holes.why: The chapter quotes Bloom's indictment of Jagger at length as the leading intellectual voice of the anti-Stones moral panic, and the next section opens by dissecting Bloom's "morally offended viewpoint."

holes.name: Aleister Crowley
holes.what: Occultist "Great Beast 666" whose Thelemic law "Do What Thou Wilt" espoused a form of anarchism and whose Lucifer was the light-bearing god rather than Christianity's dark devil.
holes.why: The chapter makes Crowley, through Kenneth Anger, the source of the Stones' occult persona and of the Lucifer Rising project built around Jagger as a latter-day Lucifer.

holes.name: William Blake
holes.what: Romantic poet-painter whose Marriage of Heaven and Hell made the Devil a positive force of energy, emotion and creativity, and held that "the road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom."
holes.why: The chapter's "Flowers of Evil" section uses Blake's philosophy of energy and his attack on Augustine's Original Sin as the principal source of the Romantic evil the Stones channeled.

holes.name: Charles Baudelaire
holes.what: French Romantic poet whose Flowers of Evil and "Litanies to Satan" found in Satan a symbol of political revolution and dark beauty, arguing that humans, not Satan, create hell on earth.
holes.why: The chapter reports Jagger's own admission that "Sympathy for the Devil" came from "an old idea of Baudelaire's," making him the song's acknowledged philosophical source.

holes.name: Georges Bataille
holes.what: French philosopher of excess who named humanity's surplus energy "the accursed share" and analyzed in clinical detail the proximity of eroticism, sacrifice and death.
holes.why: Chapter 22's account of the sex-and-death fusion in ancient ritual frenzy and in the Stones' debauchery rests directly on Bataille's "accursed share," which the chapter introduces by name.
